old: **In this way, the pupil's own defining qualities — appropriate to receiving proper instruction from a qualified Acharya (teacher) — are established for the pupil's benefit as well.** This too is a distinct benefit — namely, the teaching of the Veda's own meaning becomes possible. Regarding this matter, the Veda-mantra taken up here for illustration [is the one whose meaning we've been examining]: whatever action the Acharya takes with his student — whether accepting him for instruction, guiding his conduct, or teaching him respectfully — through all such acts, he cultivates the qualities properly belonging to a genuine teacher. **The verse states**: whether it be a whole [verse] or half, if the student cannot grasp it properly, or if he errs in reciting the mantra, [the teacher should not cause him pain by harsh correction] — thus it is said. Because [causing pain to a student] is not consistent with proper conduct, one should not [act this way]. **Furthermore**: the deity presiding over knowledge (Sarasvati/Vagdevata) is spoken of as the fitting recipient of the offering here — and it is entirely proper that the student's own conduct be modeled after this virtue.
new: **This is the meaning of the second mantra: in the first mantra the teacher was given the rules he is to follow in teaching the Veda; this mantra states the pupil's duties. The word the original uses for "true" is the negative of "vitatha"; "vitatha" is an untrue utterance from which no human end is gained, that is, the sentences used in worldly dealings; the opposite, "avitatha", is the true Vedic utterance that serves the human end. With such Vedic words, nectar in nature, the teacher fills the pupil's ears, that is, he always teaches him; here, by the force of the prefix, another sense must be given to the root meaning "to fill": he who always makes the pupil hear the Veda. And if the pupil is dull-witted, that is, unable to take in even half a Rik or a Rik, he teaches him a pāda of the Rik, or a part of a pāda, according to his power of understanding, so that no trouble is caused to him.**

old: **Why should we take the trouble to know a mantra's rishi?** The reason is stated as follows: those who compose or discover [a mantra] at the very beginning — that is, at the start of creation (or, according to some, at the start of the cosmic cycle) — are called the rishis for that mantra. It is they who hold the credit for it. Later, brahmins who wish to make use of that mantra, out of respect and gratitude toward that rishi, must know and recite his name whenever they recite the mantra, so that the rishi remains pleased. Elsewhere, it is likewise stated that the rishi is himself worthy of honour precisely because of this connection to the mantra.
new: **The reason why rishis are called rishis is now given.** At the beginning of the yuga (or at the beginning of creation) certain men practised austerity (tapas) in order to obtain the Veda. The self-existent Veda-Purusha came to them. And in the Taittiriya Aranyaka (2-9) it is said, in the passage quoted above, that at the beginning of the kalpa Brahmins were created by the Supreme Lord; since they were not born from a womb as we are, they were called Ajas (the unborn). While such unborn and pure Brahmins were performing austerity directed to the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the world, the Supreme Lord appeared before them after some time, to favour them, and taught them the Veda. Because the Supreme Lord came to them, that is, in keeping with the meaning of the root (ṛṣ, to go), the Lord went to them, they came to be called rishis. Afterwards the other great souls born in the world, who became seers of Vedic mantras by realising the Lord through austerity and the like, were also called rishis. This is the reason for the name. Moreover, they became famous as rishis because by the grace of the Supreme Lord they obtained, at the beginning of the kalpa, as a vision, the knowledge of the Veda, which cannot be known through the senses and the like. When at the end of a yuga the world is absorbed in the Supreme Self, the Vedas and the other sciences are also merged in him; so at the beginning of the next yuga the Brahmins created anew performed austerity and by the grace of the Supreme Lord regained the vanished Vedas and the Itihasas: so says a Puranic text.
